w: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Palermo built its seat around one long argument with itself: Norman bones, Islamic details, Gothic remnants, then an 18th-century remodel that tried to tidy the whole thing up. The patchwork of eras looks less like a single church than several centuries disagreeing under one dome.
s: A Norman-Gothic-Baroque church arguing with itself.
_facts: Cathedral church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Palermo, dedicated to the Assumption of the Virgin Mary
Characterized by different architectural styles from a long history of additions, alterations and restorations, the last in the 18th century

w: William II of Sicily broke ground here in 1174, raising one of the finest Norman churches anywhere and dedicating it to the Virgin's Nativity. Rome elevated it to a metropolitan cathedral within a decade. Now a strand of the Arab-Norman UNESCO listing, it still runs 102 metres long under its Norman roof.
s: Norman masterpiece raised by William II in 1174.
_facts: Begun in 1174 by William II of Sicily, dedicated to the Nativity of the Virgin Mary
Elevated to metropolitan cathedral in 1182 by Pope Lucius III
Part of the Arab-Norman Palermo UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015
102 metres long and 40 metres wide

w: The Capuchin monks kept burying and dressing their dead here long after most of Europe had stopped, leaving corridors of mummified friars, nobles and children in their Sunday best. Today it stands as a somewhat macabre tourist attraction and, at the same time, an extraordinary historical record.
s: Corridors of dressed, mummified Capuchin dead.
_facts: Burial catacombs in Palermo, Sicily
Today provide a somewhat macabre tourist attraction as well as an extraordinary historical record

w: Roger II commissioned this royal chapel in 1132 and got three civilizations for the price of one: Byzantine mosaics, Norman stonework and a muqarnas ceiling carved in the Fatimid style, all under one roof built atop an older 1080s crypt. The mosaics alone were still unfinished a decade later.
s: Byzantine, Norman and Fatimid craft under one roof.
_facts: Royal chapel of the Norman Palace, mixture of Byzantine, Norman and Fatimid architectural styles
Commissioned by Roger II of Sicily in 1132, built atop an older chapel from around 1080
Mosaics only partially finished by 1143
Muqarnas ceiling of the nave shows Fatimid influence

w: Roger II's Hauteville dynasty ruled Sicily from these walls, and Frederick II later held his imperial court here too - making this, by most reckonings, the oldest royal residence still standing in Europe. Since 1946 it has swapped kings for the Sicilian Regional Assembly, still legislating inside a medieval palace.
s: Europe's oldest royal residence, still in session.
_facts: Seat of the Kings of Sicily with the Hauteville dynasty, later main seat of power for subsequent rulers
The oldest royal residence in Europe
Private residence of Kingdom of Sicily rulers and imperial seat of Frederick II and Conrad IV
Since 1946, seat of the Sicilian Regional Assembly

w: Palermo built the biggest opera house in Italy and dedicated it to King Victor Emanuel II - at its inauguration only Paris's Palais Garnier and Vienna's Hof-Opernhaus outranked it for size anywhere in Europe. It's still prized for near-perfect acoustics, a rare feat for a building of this scale.
s: Italy's biggest opera house, near-perfect acoustics.
_facts: Opera house on Piazza Verdi, dedicated to King Victor Emanuel II
The biggest opera house in Italy, third largest in Europe at inauguration after the Palais Garnier and Vienna's K.K. Hof-Opernhaus
Renowned for its perfect acoustics

w: Built for Sicily's Norman admiral, this church ended up as co-cathedral for the Italo-Albanian Catholic Church, still celebrating the Byzantine Rite in Koine Greek and Albanian centuries after Albanian exiles fled Ottoman persecution and settled here. Their icons, language and rite all left visible traces inside.
s: Byzantine Rite in Greek and Albanian, in Sicily.
_facts: Church of St Mary of the Admiral, co-cathedral to the Eparchy of Piana degli Albanesi (Italo-Albanian Catholic Church)
Liturgy in the Byzantine Rite in Koine Greek and Albanian language
Albanian exiles took refuge here from the 15th century fleeing Ottoman persecution, leaving traces in icon painting, rite and language

w: Palermo's four ancient quarters - Kalsa, Seralcadi, Albergaria and Castellammare - meet at this single Baroque crossroads, each claiming one curved corner where Via Maqueda meets the Cassaro. A fountain, three churches and the road to the cathedral all sit within a few steps - the old city compressed into one junction.
s: Four ancient quarters meet at one Baroque corner.
_facts: Officially Piazza Vigliena, considered the center of Palermo's historic quarters
Intersection of Via Maqueda and Corso Vittorio Emanuele; the four corners represent the ancient quarters Kalsa, Seralcadi, Albergaria and Castellammare
Nearby stand the church of San Giuseppe dei Padre Teatini, the Fontana Pretoria, Santa Caterina, San Cataldo and La Martorana

w: Phoenician settlers consecrated this limestone promontory to the fertility goddess Tanit; centuries later Christian hermits took over the same slopes, and Saint Rosalia - Palermo's patron saint - is said to have died in a cave near the summit. At 606 metres it remains the skyline every Palermitano recognizes.
s: Sacred to Phoenicians, home to Palermo's patron saint.
_facts: Carbonate rock promontory, 606 metres above sea level, highest peak within the city
Phoenician settlers who founded Palermo considered it sacred and established a sanctuary to the goddess Tanit; later a destination for Christian hermit monks
Home to the Sanctuary of Saint Rosalia, Palermo's patron saint, who died in a cave

w: Also called Palazzo Patella, this Kalsa-quarter palazzo now houses the Galleria Regionale della Sicilia, the island's own regional art collection. A private residence turned public gallery, tucked into Palermo's oldest waterfront district.
s: A Kalsa palazzo turned Sicily's regional gallery.
_facts: Also known as Palazzo Patella, located in the Kalsa quarter
Home to the Galleria Regionale della Sicilia, the Gallery of Art for the Sicilian region

w: Ice Age hunters scratched a rare complex of engravings into these three grottoes above Mondello beach, dated to the Epigravettian and Mesolithic - one of the Mediterranean's few known sites of this kind. Tools and bones found here now sit in Palermo's museum; the name comes from Arabic for 'the circuit'.
s: Ice Age rock art above Mondello beach.
_facts: Complex of three natural grottoes on Mount Pellegrino, engravings dated to the late Epigravettian and Mesolithic
A unique case in the panorama of prehistoric cave art in the Mediterranean
Finds now conserved in Palermo's Regional Archaeological Museum
Name comes from Arabic al-dawrah, 'the circuit'

w: Francesco Camilliani carved this fountain for a private Florentine garden in 1544 - then it was sold off wholesale, shipped south and reassembled piece by piece in Palermo three decades later. It now anchors Piazza Pretoria, one block south of the Quattro Canti crossroads, dominating the square's western flank.
s: A Florentine fountain, shipped south and rebuilt.
_facts: Monumental fountain built originally in 1544 in Florence by Francesco Camilliani
Sold, transferred and reassembled in Palermo in 1574
Dominates Piazza Pretoria on the west flank of Santa Caterina, one block from the Quattro Canti

w: Strip away the interior decoration entirely and what's left are bare Islamic domes rising over a Romanesque cloister garden, two blocks from the Royal Palace. The combination - Arab silhouette, Norman stonework, empty of ornament - has made this small former monastic church a shorthand for old Palermo itself.
s: Bare Islamic domes over a Norman cloister garden.
_facts: Ancient former monastic church in the Albergaria quarter, two blocks south of the Palazzo dei Normanni
Interior virtually devoid of decoration or furnishings
Islamic domes, Romanesque cloister ruins and garden make it a symbol of ancient Palermo

w: Palermo raised this monumental gate to celebrate Charles V's conquest of Tunis in 1535 and his visit to the Sicilian capital, planting it where the road from Monreale enters the ancient Cassaro. It still stands beside the Royal Palace, marking the old city's grand front door.
s: A gate built to celebrate conquering Tunis.
_facts: Monumental city gate, entrance of the Cassaro from the road to Monreale, beside the Palazzo dei Normanni
Built to celebrate Charles V's conquest of Tunis (1535) and his visit to the capital of the Kingdom of Sicily

w: Known locally as Casa Professa, this Baroque church at Piazza Casa Professa 21 was raised under the patronage of the Society of Jesus - one of Palermo's Jesuit strongholds, tucked into the old city's tangle of streets.
s: Casa Professa, a Jesuit Baroque stronghold.
_facts: Baroque-style Roman Catholic church established under the patronage of the Jesuit order, at Piazza Casa Professa 21
Also called Saint Mary of Jesus or the Casa Professa

w: George of Antioch, the Norman kingdom's 'admiral of admirals,' had this bridge thrown across the Oreto River - a Greek-born Christian commanding a fleet for a Norman king in an Arab city, all in one job title. It's been a UNESCO listing since 2015, part of the wider Arab-Norman Palermo site.
s: A Norman admiral's bridge, now UNESCO-listed.
_facts: Medieval bridge over the Oreto River, built during Norman Sicily by the ammiratus ammiratorum George of Antioch
Became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015 as part of Arab-Norman Palermo and the Cathedral Churches of Cefalu and Monreale

w: Thirty acres of red soil sitting on a limestone tuff base host the University of Palermo's working botanical garden and research institute - a teaching collection as much as a public one, ten metres above sea level in the heart of the city.
s: Thirty acres of teaching garden on volcanic tuff.
_facts: Botanical garden and research/educational institution of the Department of Botany, University of Palermo
Lies at 10 metres above sea level, covers about 0.12 sq km (30 acres) of red soil on a limestone tuff substratum

w: Antonino Salinas ran this museum for over forty years and then left it his entire private collection when he died in 1914 - one of Italy's richest troves of Punic and Ancient Greek art, still housed in the former Oratory of Saint Philip Neri within the Olivella monastic complex.
s: A scholar's life collection of Punic and Greek art.
_facts: One of the richest collections of Punic and Ancient Greek art in Italy, plus items on Sicily's history
Formerly the property of the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri
Named after Antonino Salinas, archaeologist and numismatist, director from 1873 until his death in 1914, who left it his major private collection
Part of the Olivella monumental complex
